89.text:
API Reference
The SDK exposes the PocketMage hardware and OS services to loaded apps through a set of component objects plus free functions. Every component is declared in pocketmage.h, the umbrella header an app includes first:
#include <pocketmage.h>

pocketmage.h pulls in every component header, config.h, the frames and assets modules, and Preferences.h. It also includes pocketmage_app_version.h when the build defines PM_TARGET_APP, so the SDK-version macros are always available to apps.
An external app does not call these C++ classes directly across the ELF boundary; it calls the flat pm_* C ABI that projects them. See The C ABI (pm_*) below, and the complete function index for every wrapper and its signature.
Compile target
config.h requires exactly one of these to be defined, and fails the build otherwise:



Macro
Meaning




PM_TARGET_HOST
the PocketMageOS firmware links the SDK in-process


PM_TARGET_APP
an external app compiled to a loadable .app.elf



The two are mutually exclusive; defining both is a build error. Apps declare PM_TARGET_APP (see Building an app).
The singleton pattern
Most components are owned by a single global instance created inside the SDK and reached through a global accessor function. The accessor returns a reference; null checks are unnecessary once the component’s setup*() call has run in PocketMage_INIT().

The frames component is used by the OS’s built-in apps. Third-party apps start from the simpler primitives in oled, eink, font, and layout.
The C ABI (pm_*)
The accessors and classes above are the host-side API. The SDK compiles the firmware with the C++ API directly, but an external ELF app cannot: it links -nostdlib and resolves symbols by name at load time, so the app-facing surface is a flat C ABI, the pm_* functions, generated from the C++ classes by tools/gen_app_api.py. An app includes the generated header through pm_app_api.h:
#include <pm_app_api.h>

The generator projects each exported C++ method to one C function by a fixed set of rules:



C++ shape
C projection




ClassName::method(args)
pm_<module>_<method>(args) on the module’s singleton


String parameter or return
const char* (returns point into the string pool, below)


enum parameter or return
plain int (values in SDK declaration order)


std::vector<T> return
a _count function plus a _get(index, out, out_size) pair


scalar out-parameter by reference
T* out-pointer



Enums become integers with generated value tables: pm_target, pm_style, pm_lang, pm_refresh, and pm_jingle. PM_APP_API_ABI tracks incompatible changes to this surface; an app compares it against pm_app_abi() at startup, and pocketmage_sdk_version (via pm_host_sdk_version()) gives the running host’s SDK version.
Every const char* return points into a shared rotating string pool: four 256-byte slots, where the fifth string-returning call overwrites the first. Copy a returned string before making further SDK calls if you need to keep it. Functions that can return arbitrary length write into a caller-owned buffer instead. The full rule and the per-function list are in the function index.
The pm_* names are the app’s real dependency contract and are gated at load time against the curated host surface; see symbols.md. Each component page below documents its pm_* wrappers alongside the C++ class they project.
Reading a component page
Every API page follows the same shape:

Access: how the object is reached and what to include.
Lifecycle: the setup*() call in PocketMage_INIT() that must run first, and how the component behaves across deep sleep and app load.
Reference: one section per class or function. Signatures are verbatim from the headers; notes state runtime behavior, threading constraints, and return values.
Example: a minimal snippet, usually drawing to one of the two displays.

Threading notes matter: the E-Ink panel is guarded by a recursive mutex and refreshed from a background task; code runnin

System API
The system module owns the board bring-up, the CPU clock, deep sleep, the power button, and the shared globals (battState, allLines, CurrentAppState, the SPI buses, and NVS prefs). Apps use it for power management and boot-time configuration; the OS uses it for full bring-up.
Access
#include <pocketmage.h>

Shared globals
pocketmage_globals defines the state both the OS and apps link against.
SPI and filesystem
extern SPIClass* vspi;    // the global SPI on SPI_SCK/SPI_MOSI
extern SPIClass* hspi;
extern fs::FS*   global_fs;  // active filesystem (SD_MMC or SD)

PocketMage_INIT wires vspi = &SPI and pins the pins documented in configuration.
NVS
extern Preferences prefs;   // "PocketMage" namespace

The shared Preferences handle. pocketmage::loadSettings() reads the persistent toggles into the config.h globals (TIMEOUT, SAVE_POWER, FAST_REFRESH, OLED_BRIGHTNESS, the UI language, …); an app that reads preferences uses prefs directly with the same namespace.
App state
enum AppState { HOME, TXT, FILEWIZ, USB_APP, COMM, SETTINGS, TASKS,
                CALENDAR, JOURNAL, LEXICON, APPLOADER, TERMINAL,
                ONBOARDING, ELFAPP };
extern AppState CurrentAppState;

The OS’s app dispatch enum. ELFAPP is the state set while a loaded ELF app is running; the OS restores HOME when it exits.
Keyboard state
enum KBState { NORMAL, SHIFT, FUNC, FN_SHIFT };

The keyboard modifier state, mirrored by KB().setKeyboardState().
pocketmage:: namespace
namespace pocketmage {
  void loadSettings();          // load NVS settings into the config.h globals
  void recoverFromCrash();      // reset app state after a panic/watchdog
  void checkRTCPowerLoss();     // baseline the RTC when it has lost power
}


loadSettings() reads every persistent toggle from prefs and sets the UI language. Apps call it during APP_INIT (the OS reaches it via PocketMage_INIT on the host path).
recoverFromCrash() checks the ESP reset reason and, on panic or watchdog reset, resets CurrentAppState to HOME and clears the editing-file pointer so the device boots clean.
checkRTCPowerLoss() re-baselines the RTC when its power was lost.

Battery helper
inline float getBatteryVoltage() {
  return (analogRead(BAT_SENS) * (3.3 / 4095.0) * 2) + 0.2;
}

battState (0 through 5) indexes the battery bitmaps used by the OLED status line (oled, assets).
CPU speed
void pocketmage::setCpuSpeed(int newFreq);

Clamps to the valid S3 frequencies {240, 160, 80, 40, 20, 10} and returns early if the CPU is already there. WiFi stalls below 240 MHz on the S3, so a request that would drop the clock below WIFI_CPU_FREQ_MHZ (240) while P_WIFI is not Off is ignored. POWER_SAVE_FREQ (40) is the OS’s idle speed; sysMessage and the WiFi service bump back to 240 when they need it.
Scope guard
class pocketmage::ScopedCpuBoost {
public:
  ScopedCpuBoost();            // raises to 240 MHz if not already there
  ~ScopedCpuBoost();           // restores the previous frequency
};

Non-copyable RAII. Usable as a stack local around a latency-critical section.
Deep sleep
void pocketmage::deepSleep(bool alternateScreenSaver = false);

Full power-down sequence:

Power-saves the OLED.
Stops the einkHandlerTask under the panel lock, so an in-flight refresh completes.
Plays Jingles::Shutdown.
Draws a screensaver (custom /assets/backgrounds/*.bin, else a random built-in) at rotation 3, or the alternate screensaver when asked. SAVE_POWER drops the CPU to POWER_SAVE_FREQ for the draw.
Clears the buffer, hibernates the panel, unlocks it.
Persists CurrentAppState, the editing file, and clears the seamless reboot flag.
On production hardware, isolates the peripheral pins with setLoadSwitch(false) (GPIO hold + gpio_deep_sleep_hold_en).
esp_deep_sleep_start().

Wake is on the KB_IRQ falling edge (configured in PocketMage_INIT). Resume re-runs PocketMage_INIT, which clears the pin holds and re-inits peripherals.
Power button
void IRAM_ATTR pocketmage::PWR_BTN_irq();
extern volatile bool PWR_BTN_event;

The FALLING-edge interrupt service routine sets PWR_BTN_event. The OS consumes it for wake/shutdown handling; holding PWR_BTN for 3 seconds while awake raises the hard-reset-to-home path (resetRequested, see the hardReset task). SDActive, mscEnabled, and sinkEnabled are the status-line indicators apps toggle for long I/O.
Bring-up
void PocketMage_INIT();

The one-call bring-up: release GPIO holds, enable the load switch (production), read the seamless reboot flag, FontEngine::init(), Serial, Wire (plus Wire1 on production), the global SPI, the keyboard wake pin, setupOled(), setupKB(), setupEink(), setupSD(), power-button interrupt + MP2722 power init, the hard-reset task, the power-save clock, setupTouch(), setupClock(), the random seed, settings load, crash recovery, setupBZ() + startup jingle, the WiFi service (host only), key flush, then the app hook APP_INIT() (app builds). Apps do not call it; it runs as part of the OS or the app entry shim.

198.title: App binary contract (ABI)
198.text:
App binary contract (ABI)
The loader accepts exactly one thing: a 32-bit ET_DYN ELF, little-endian, entry app_main. Anything else fails to load. Build and packaging mechanics live in build.md; the symbol surface in symbols.md; the overlay sidecar that ships beside the ELF in overlay.md.
Format

e_ident[EI_CLASS] = ELFCLASS32
e_ident[EI_DATA] = ELFDATA2LSB
e_type = ET_DYN (position independent)
entry = the app_main symbol

The loader reads the ELF structures with plain native reads. No byte swapping, no endianness validation. A big-endian file decodes into garbage and the load fails, which is why app.mk asserts endianness after link and refuses to keep a bad artifact.
Only the espressif xtensa-esp-elf toolchain emits output the loader can read. The PlatformIO package emits the wrong byte order and is unusable for apps; see build.md for install paths.
Entry point
The host looks up app_main by name and runs it on core 1 in a dedicated task with a 16 KB stack:
int main(int argc, char **argv);   // renamed to app_main at build time

The build passes -Dmain=app_main -e app_main, so an app writes its entry with C linkage:
extern "C" int main(int argc, char **argv)

The runner passes four arguments, taken from the install record and the app.properties manifest:



Index
Value




argv[0]
app name (manifest name, else base name)


argv[1]
absolute path of the loaded ELF


argv[2]
app version string (manifest version)


argv[3]
author string (manifest author)



Returning from main tears the app down: the overlay is unloaded, the base image is deinitialized, and control returns to the OS, which reopens HOME. There is no run-forever semantics. A UI app hands control back through the SDK/host API cooperatively, then returns. A main that never returns leaks the run task.
How loading works
Loading is two stages: a base relocation with esp_elf, then an overlay pass with elf_overlay. The runner is src/elf_runner.cpp.

The scoped symbol resolver is installed first, because relocation is what asks the host to resolve each undefined symbol (see symbols.md). esp_elf_init then esp_elf_relocate_source relocate the base image. The ELF is streamed by offset from the SD file, so the whole file is never held in RAM; only transient section buffers add to the peak.
Relocated .text lands in MALLOC_CAP_EXEC memory so code is executable on the S3; data and rodata land in MALLOC_CAP_8BIT DRAM. Code in PSRAM is not executable on the ESP32-S3, app or firmware.
The <name>.elfo sidecar is located next to the ELF and loaded by elf_overlay, which pages overlay .text bodies into a pool of exec-RAM frames on demand, patches ISA-specific literal loads at page-in, applies redirects so resident calls route through stubs, and redirects the entry point through its stub. If no sidecar is present the app runs unredirected from the base relocation. The blob format and the full page-in sequence are in overlay.md.

The esp_elf loader does not run relocation-time constructors, so any .init_array the app links in is never executed. Keep the app free of constructor sections (-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics are on by default in app.mk); pm check warns if a .init_array slips in. Do not rely on static-construction order at load time.
Apps link -nostdlib: no newlib, no libstdc++, no SDK copy in the ELF. Everything an app references must resolve at load time from the host. Linking newlib into the app is wasteful and collides with host globals. Don’t.
Third-party libraries
An app can link any C or C++ library that compiles for Xtensa. The host exports the C and C++ runtime symbols, so a library’s references to malloc, memcpy, operator new, and the soft-float helpers resolve against the host instead of needing a copy in the app.
Source is compiled into the app by overriding APP_SRCS:
APP_SRCS = main.cpp third_party/cJSON.c

That keeps the app small. tools/app.mk links with -Os, -ffunction-sections, --gc-sections and --strip-all, so a library’s unused functions are dropped: cJSON linked into an app comes to 5.2 KB rather than the size of its source.
Two limits worth knowing. The host exports runtime symbols the firmware already links, so a library needing a function nothing in the firmware uses will not resolve until the host exports it deliberately. And symbol counts depend on the app’s own optimization level: the same std::vector source at -O0 wants 13 host symbols, at -Os it wants 7. app.mk uses -Os.
sscanf is the one common libc function the host does not export. It exists in newlib but nothing in the firmware references it, so --gc-sections dropped it, and referencing it pulls in about 190 KB of stdio reentrancy. Prefer strtod or strtol in app code and in vendored libraries. See symbols.md.
Calling the SDK from an app
An app includes one header and calls plain C functions:
#include <pm_app_api.h>

pm_i18n_set_language(PM_LANG_ENGLISH);
int w = pm_text_width(2, "Hello", 2);
pm_oled_sysmsg("saved", 1500);

211.title: Building an app
211.text:
Building an app
The whole build system is one Makefile that includes the SDK recipe in tools/app.mk.
Project layout
myapp/
  Makefile         # include of tools/app.mk
  main.cpp
  myapp_ICON.bin   # 40x40 icon, see Icon below
  app.properties   # optional manifest: name, version, author, scope
  src/i18n/        # optional app translation catalog

SDK_ROOT ?= $(abspath ../..)      # path to this repo
include $(SDK_ROOT)/tools/app.mk

Everything is overridable on the command line or in the Makefile: APP_SRCS (default main.cpp), APP_NAME (default the directory basename), APP_BUILD_DIR (default build), XTENSA_CXX (default: probed toolchain).
Toolchain



Requirement
Value




Compiler
espressif xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++


Output
little-endian (required by the loader)



The PlatformIO toolchain-xtensa-esp32s3 package emits big-endian ELFs and is unusable for apps; if it is the only compiler found, app.mk fails the build with a clear error. Install the espressif toolchain so it lands at one of the probed paths (newest first):
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-15.2.0_20251204/xtensa-esp-elf/bin
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-14.2.0_20251107/xtensa-esp-elf/bin
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-14.2.0_20241119/xtensa-esp-elf/bin

esp-15.2.0_20251204 is the one SDK CI pins (URL and SHA256). It is the easiest known-good install:
VER=esp-15.2.0_20251204
SHA=3d50f5cd5f173acfd524e07c1cd69bc99585731a415ca2e5bce879997fe602b8
URL="https://github.com/espressif/crosstool-NG/releases/download/$VER/xtensa-esp-elf-15.2.0_20251204-x86_64-linux-gnu.tar.xz"
mkdir -p "$HOME/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/$VER"
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/xtensa-esp-elf.tar.xz "$URL"
echo "$SHA  /tmp/xtensa-esp-elf.tar.xz" | sha256sum -c -
tar -xJf /tmp/xtensa-esp-elf.tar.xz -C "$HOME/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/$VER"

The example builds with any probed version. The host OS pins its own toolchain independently of the SDK.
Targets



Target
Result




make
Builds build/<name>.app.elf (stripped, endianness-asserted) and build/<name>.elfo (the overlay sidecar)


make overlay
Builds only build/<name>.elfo


make check
Prints the entry point and every undefined symbol (the app’s host dependency list). Informational; the enforcing gate is pm check


make pack
Builds build/<name>.tar with <name>.app.elf, <name>.elfo, <name>_ICON.bin, and app.properties when present (see publishing)


make pm-info
Prints the resolved paths and toolchain the pm CLI reads


make clean
Removes build/



The endianness assertion runs after every link. A big-endian artifact gets deleted and the build fails.
Overlay emission
Alongside the ELF, make produces build/<name>.elfo, the overlay blob the host pages into executable RAM at load time. It is built from the unstripped link output in two steps:
elf_overlay_relink <name>.app.tool <name>.relk
elf_overlay_emit   <name>.relk     <name>.elfo

Both tools must be on PATH. They come from an elf_overlay checkout, built with CMake (cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build --target elf_overlay_relink elf_overlay_emit), then the build directory added to PATH. Override ELF_OVERLAY_RELINK and ELF_OVERLAY_EMIT to point at specific binaries. The format and the device-side load sequence are in overlay.md.
Entry point
extern "C" int main(int argc, char **argv), renamed to app_main via -Dmain=app_main -e app_main. See app-abi.md for the full contract. Everything the app calls resolves from the host at load time, so keep the undefined-symbol list (from make check) small and intentional; see symbols.md.
Compiler flags
The SDK builds with -Wall -Wextra, exceptions and RTTI disabled, and hidden visibility. Keep the code warning-free.
app.mk injects PM_SDK_VERSION plus PM_SDK_VERSION_MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH from the repo VERSION file, so an app always sees POCKETMAGE_SDK_VERSION_* in pocketmage_app_version.h alongside the host-exported string literal pocketmage_sdk_version; see app-abi.md.
Icon
<name>_ICON.bin is a 200-byte file: a 40x40, 1-bit-per-pixel bitmap (5 bytes per row, 8 pixels per byte), drawn by the OS as the app icon. make pack requires the file next to the Makefile and errors without it. The OS falls back to a default icon only for an installed app that has none.
Translations
An app that shows strings uses its own catalog; see i18n.md. The short version: put a src/i18n/ tree in your app and merge it via the generator the way platformio.ini shows in that doc.
Before you ship
Run make clean all then pm check before every commit; pm check is the gate CI runs, and --host-elf <firmware.elf> pins the host export surface exactly (see symbols.md). make pack is the deliverable; verify the tar’s members with tar -tf build/<name>.tar. It should list <name>.app.elf, <name>.elfo, <name>_ICON.bin, and app.properties.
pm new myapp scaffolds from the official PocketMage_App

222.title: pm CLI
222.text:
pm CLI
pm is the developer-facing wrapper around the SDK build. It drives the same make contract documented in build.md, adds the enforcing dependency gate, and handles scaffolding and release bookkeeping. Everything pm does can be done with make and the raw tools; pm is the ergonomic path and is what CI runs.
Install
The CLI ships with the SDK as the pocketmage-sdk distribution. Install it from the SDK repo root:
pip install -e .     # editable: pm tracks the checkout it was installed from
pm --help

An editable install (-e) links pm to the checkout so edits to tools/ take effect without reinstalling. A plain pip install . copies the package into site-packages instead; use that when you do not have a persistent checkout to track.
It shells out to make and the Xtensa toolchain, so an app build still needs the pinned espressif toolchain on the machine (see get-started/toolchain).
If the editable checkout is later moved or deleted, the next pm invocation detects the orphaned install, locates a live checkout, and offers to reinstall rather than failing with an import error. See pm doctor and pm update-sdk below.
Global options



Option
Effect




--ci
plain output, no ANSI escapes


--no-color
alias for --ci


--theme NAME
output theme: default, mono, or pastel



CI mode also turns on automatically when CI or NO_COLOR is set in the environment.
Commands
pm new <name> [dest]
Scaffolds a new app from the official PocketMage_App template into dest (default: the current directory). Replace the scaffolded assets/icon.png with your own 40x40 artwork to change the APPLOADER card icon. The next steps are pm build --pack then pm check.
pm build [app_dir] [--clean] [--pack]
Builds the app via make. --clean runs make clean first; --pack also builds the delivery tar. Requires the Xtensa toolchain to be present and resolves the same paths make pm-info prints. Produces build/<name>.app.elf and build/<name>.elfo.
pm check [app_dir] [--host-elf ELF] [--readelf BIN]
The enforcing dependency gate. Reads the built ELF’s undefined-symbol list and classifies each symbol against the curated host surface (see symbols.md):

resolvable - in the curated surface (symbols.list plus host_baseline.list). Passes.
unconfirmed - outside the curated surface. Needs --host-elf <firmware.elf> to confirm against the actual host export table; without it, check reports the app as unconfirmed and exits non-zero.
broken - not resolvable by the host. The load would fail. Exits non-zero.

check also surfaces two warnings that do not fail the gate on their own:

app_main not present in the shipped ELF’s symbol table. The entry is still trusted because it is linker-pinned with -e app_main; a post-link strip removed the name.
A non-empty .init_array. The app links static constructors, and the host’s esp_elf loader does not run them. Do not rely on static construction at load time.

The icon is validated as part of the gate; an invalid icon fails the check.
pm pack [app_dir]
Builds the delivery tar via make pack. The tar holds <name>.app.elf, <name>.elfo, <name>_ICON.bin, and app.properties when present. See publishing.
pm exports [--host LIST] [--all]
Reconciles the SDK’s symbols.list against a PocketMageOS src/ELF_SYMS/host_exports.list. Every curated symbol must be exported by the host; a curated symbol the host does not export is an error to fix on the OS side, not in symbols.list. --host points at a specific host list (default: a sibling PocketMageOS checkout). --all additionally lists host exports that sit outside the curated surface, as advisory output.
pm release {major|minor|patch} [--message TEXT]
Bumps the SDK release version. Updates VERSION, pocketmage_globals.cpp, library.json, and CHANGELOG.md; --message files a feature line under the new version in the changelog. It does not commit or tag; commit the bump and tag the release yourself when ready.
pm version
Prints pocketmage_sdk_version, the version string the host exports and apps compare against at startup.
pm doctor
Reports the health of the pm install and the SDK checkout it resolves. It prints the interpreter running pm, the installed distribution version and mode (editable or regular), the resolved SDK checkout and its VERSION, and, for an editable install, the directory the install is linked to. It flags three failures and exits non-zero on any of them:

The editable target no longer exists; the install is orphaned.
The tools package is not importable in this interpreter.
The installed CLI version does not match the checkout’s VERSION.

When it finds a problem it prints the exact reinstall command and points at pm update-sdk. Run pm doctor first whenever pm behaves unexpectedly.
pm update-sdk / pm update-self
Reinstalls pm against a live SDK checkout, repairing an orphaned editable install or clearing version skew. The two names are the same command. It resolves the checkout from --sdk <path>, then PM_SDK_ROOT, then an upward walk from

238.title: Your first app
238.text:
Your first app
This walks the full path from an empty directory to an app running on the device. It assumes the toolchain is installed.
1. Scaffold
pm new hello
cd hello

pm new clones the official PocketMage_App template. You get a Makefile that includes tools/app.mk, a main.cpp with an app_main entry, an icon, and an app.properties manifest.
The entry point is app_main, written with C linkage so the mangled name matches the -e app_main linker entry. An app calls the flat pm_* C API from pm_app_api.h, not the C++ singletons; the app links -nostdlib and resolves every pm_* symbol from the host at load time:
#include "pm_app_api.h"

extern "C" int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    const char *name = argc > 0 && argv[0] ? argv[0] : "hello";
    pm_oled_sysmsg(name, 1500);
    return 0;   // returning hands control back to the OS
}

The runner passes four arguments: argv[0] is the app name, argv[1] the absolute ELF path, argv[2] the version string, and argv[3] the author, all taken from the install record and the manifest. See app-abi.md.
2. Build
pm build --pack

This produces build/hello.app.elf (the relocatable ELF), build/hello.elfo (the overlay sidecar), and build/hello.tar (the delivery package). Under the hood it runs make all pack; the targets are in build.md.
3. Gate
pm check

pm check reads the app’s undefined-symbol list, which is its real dependency contract because the app links -nostdlib, and classifies every symbol against the host surface. A green result means the host resolves everything. For an exact result against a specific firmware, pass the host ELF:
pm check --host-elf /path/to/firmware.elf

The symbol model is in symbols.md; the gate’s warnings and exit codes are in cli.md.
4. Inspect the package
tar -tf build/hello.tar

It should list hello.app.elf, hello.elfo, hello_ICON.bin, and app.properties. The packaging rules are in publishing.
5. Install on the device

Copy build/hello.tar onto the SD card at /apps/hello.tar, usually over USB.
On the device, open the app loader and use the swap action to install the tar into one of the four slots.
Launch it from the home screen with A, B, C, or D, or from the loader.

Delete the tar from /apps after a successful install to free space on the card. The device-side install behavior is owned by the PocketMageOS docs.

Draw to the displays: Rendering.
Browse the API: Function index.

246.title: Get Started
246.text:
Get Started
A PocketMage app is a standalone ELF the device loads and runs at runtime. There is no firmware reflash: you build an ELF, pack it with an overlay sidecar and an icon, copy the tar onto the SD card, and install it through the on-device app loader. The host resolves everything the app references, from malloc to the pm_* API, at load time.
This section takes you from nothing to a running app in two steps.
Install the toolchain - the pinned espressif Xtensa compiler, the elf_overlay host tools, and the pm CLI.
Build your first app - scaffold, build, gate, pack, and install.

How the pieces fit



Piece
Role

the app-facing contract: headers, the pm_* ABI, the build recipe, the base i18n catalog


Xtensa toolchain
compiles and links the app into a 32-bit ET_DYN ELF


elf_overlay tools
turn the link output into the .elfo overlay sidecar


pm CLI
scaffolds, builds, gates, and packs (wraps make)


App template
the starting point pm new clones from



Where to go next

The whole app model, end to end: Making an app.
The binary contract the loader enforces: App ABI.
Every function an app can call: Function index.

250.title: Install the toolchain
250.text:
Install the toolchain
An app build needs three things on the machine: the espressif Xtensa compiler, the elf_overlay host tools, and the pm CLI. Only the espressif toolchain produces output the loader can read; the PlatformIO Xtensa package emits the wrong byte order and is unusable for apps.
Xtensa compiler
The build targets the espressif xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++ toolchain. app.mk probes for it in the espressif install directory, newest to oldest, then the PlatformIO package, then PATH:
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-15.2.0_20251204/xtensa-esp-elf/bin
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-14.2.0_20251107/xtensa-esp-elf/bin
~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-14.2.0_20241119/xtensa-esp-elf/bin
~/.platformio/packages/toolchain-xtensa-esp32s3/bin

The pinned release is esp-15.2.0_20251204. The simplest way to get it is through ESP-IDF’s installer, which places it under ~/.espressif. If you have an existing install elsewhere, point the build at it:
make XTENSA_CXX=/path/to/xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++

XTENSA_STRIP and XTENSA_READELF are derived from XTENSA_CXX unless set.
Verify the compiler resolves:
make -C <app> pm-info     # prints the resolved toolchain and paths

elf_overlay host tools
The build emits the .elfo overlay sidecar with two host tools, elf_overlay_relink and elf_overlay_emit, which must be on PATH. Build them from an elf_overlay checkout:
git clone https://github.com/TalismanDesign/elf_overlay
cd elf_overlay
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --target elf_overlay_relink elf_overlay_emit
export PATH="$PWD/build:$PATH"

Override the tool paths instead of using PATH with ELF_OVERLAY_RELINK and ELF_OVERLAY_EMIT. The overlay format itself is documented in overlay.md.
pm CLI
The pm CLI ships with the SDK as the pocketmage-sdk distribution. Install it editable from the SDK repo root so pm tracks the checkout:
pip install -e .     # editable: pm tracks the checkout it was installed from
pm --help

A plain pip install . copies the package into site-packages instead; use that when you do not have a persistent checkout to track. If an editable checkout is later moved or deleted, pm detects the orphaned install and offers to reinstall rather than failing with an import error (see pm doctor).
pm wraps the same make contract and adds the enforcing dependency gate. The full command surface is in cli.md. Icon validation uses Pillow, so install it if you want pm check to validate the icon:
pip install Pillow

Verify
pm doctor
pm new hello
cd hello
pm build --pack
pm check

pm doctor confirms the install is healthy and resolves a live SDK checkout before you build. A green pm check means every symbol the app references resolves against the host surface, and the app is ready to install. If any of these steps fail, see Troubleshooting.

256.title: Glossary
256.text:
Glossary
The terms below mean exactly one thing across these docs. Where a concept has its own page, the definition links to it.
App. A standalone 32-bit ET_DYN ELF the host loads and runs in-process at runtime. Links -nostdlib; resolves everything from the host. See App ABI.
app_main. The app entry point. Written as main with C linkage; the build renames it to app_main with -Dmain=app_main -e app_main. Runs on core 1 in a 16 KB task. See App ABI.
app.properties. The optional per-app manifest: name, version, author, and scope. Shipped in the tar and copied to the slot; the first three reach app_main as argv. See App ABI and per-app scope.
APPLOADER. The on-device installer. Extracts a /apps/*.tar, finds the *.app.elf, and installs it with its icon and manifest into one of four slots. See publishing.
Curated surface. The union of symbols.list and host_baseline.list: the set of symbols an app may resolve against. See symbols.md.
ELFO / .elfo. The overlay blob that ships beside each app ELF. Magic ELFO, ISA-tagged, carrying overlay bodies, stubs, and relocation patch tables. See overlay.md.
elf_overlay. The ISA-abstracted overlay runtime that pages app .text bodies into executable RAM and patches ISA-specific literal loads at page-in. Sits next to esp_elf. See overlay.md.
esp_elf. The base ELF relocator. Relocates the app image streamed from SD, then hands off to elf_overlay for the overlay pass. See App ABI.
gen_app_api.py. The generator that walks the SDK headers and projects each C++ method to a pm_* C wrapper, writing the names into symbols.list and the host host_exports.list. See symbols.md.
Host. The PocketMageOS firmware. It owns the hardware, exports the symbol surface, and runs apps in-process. The device side is documented in the PocketMageOS docs.
host_baseline.list. The committed list of C/C++ runtime, newlib, and POSIX symbols the firmware exports unconditionally. Generated from the firmware export table; part of the curated surface. See symbols.md.
ISA. Instruction set architecture. PocketMage runs on Xtensa (ESP32-S3); elf_overlay also has a RISC-V backend. The ELFO header is ISA-tagged and a blob loads only on its ISA. See overlay.md.
MALLOC_CAP_EXEC. Heap capability for memory the instruction bus can fetch. Relocated and paged-in .text lands here; it is scarce, which is why the overlay model pages bodies in on demand. Code in PSRAM is not executable on the S3.
Overlay body. One .text image paged into an exec-RAM frame on demand. A body must fit in a single frame. See overlay.md.
pm_* ABI. The flat C ABI an app calls, generated from the SDK’s C++ classes. Declared in pm_sdk_app.h, pulled in through pm_app_api.h. See the function index.
PM_APP_API_ABI. The ABI version an app compares against pm_app_abi() at startup to confirm it was built against a compatible surface.
pocketmage_sdk_version. The version string the host exports and apps read to check compatibility at runtime. Bumped by pm release.
Scope. The app.properties field that restricts which pm_* symbols an app may resolve (default all). An out-of-scope pm_* reference fails the load. See per-app scope.
Slot. One of four install locations on the SD card (/apps/slot1 through /apps/slot4), tracked in NVS. Launched from HOME with A-D.
String pool. The rotating buffer backing pm_* const char* returns: four 256-byte slots, the fifth string-returning call overwrites the first. Copy a returned string before further SDK calls. See function index.
Stub. The small entry/leave code in the ELFO blob that pages an overlay body in on first call and drops its frame refcount on return. See overlay.md.
Target. The compile mode, exactly one of PM_TARGET_HOST (firmware) or PM_TARGET_APP (external app), enforced by config.h. See API overview.

258.title: Internationalization
258.text:
Internationalization
PocketMage translates every user-facing string through a single merged catalog. The SDK owns the base catalog of its own strings; an app ships its own catalog, and the two merge at build time into one enum and one set of string tables. This guide covers the app side, start to finish. The generator, the merge rules, and the validation it enforces are the reference material in i18n catalogs.
Add a catalog to your app
Create one catalog directory with a subdirectory per language, named by the language code. en is required and defines the order of the strings your catalog contributes:
myapp/src/i18n/
  en/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.aliases

Each string is a standard gettext entry. msgctxt is the string’s StringID enum name, msgid is the English text, and msgstr is the translation:
msgctxt "STR_MYAPP_HELLO"
msgid "Hello"
msgstr "Bonjour"

Keep your msgctxt names in your own namespace (for example STR_MYAPP_*). They must be globally unique across the merged catalogs; reusing a name the SDK already defines is a build error. A language missing from your catalog falls back to its English text, so an English-only catalog is valid.
Wire it into the build
Point the generator at both your catalog and the SDK base catalog from your app’s platformio.ini; the generator doubles as the build hook:
extra_scripts = pre:lib/PocketMage_SDK/pocketmage_i18n/tools/gen_i18n.py

custom_i18n_catalogs =
    lib/PocketMage_SDK/pocketmage_i18n/languages
    src/i18n
custom_i18n_out_dir = .pio/build/${PIOENV}/i18n

The base catalog must come first. The merge keeps base strings first and appends your catalog after, so your strings never shift the base enum values. The generated files are build artifacts and are never committed.
Resolve strings at runtime
The runtime engine is the I18n singleton, exposed to apps through the pm_* i18n API. Set the active language, then fetch strings by their enum:
pm_i18n_set_language_by_code("fr");
const char *hello = pm_i18n_get(STR_MYAPP_HELLO);

The indexed helpers resolve names from fixed ranges in the base catalog: pm_i18n_month_name, pm_i18n_day_name, pm_i18n_app_name, and pm_i18n_kb_app_name. The full runtime surface is on the i18n (runtime) API page.
Returned strings point into the shared rotating string pool, so copy a string before further SDK calls if you need to keep it. See the string return lifetime note.
Add a language
Append the language code to the base catalog’s en file # Languages: directive and add that language’s directory to each catalog that translates it. Never reorder existing languages: the index is the value stored in NVS. The full rules, including aliases for command input and the validation the generator enforces, are in i18n catalogs.

272.title: App lifecycle
272.text:
App lifecycle
A PocketMage app is a plugin that runs inside the host firmware’s address space. Understanding where the app boundaries are is the whole battle: the app is a normal main, everything it touches comes from the host, and “exiting” is a return.
The entry point
The ELF entry is app_main, produced by the build recipe’s -Dmain=app_main -e app_main. Because an app is truly a freestanding ELF, the canonical program name is kept by writing:
extern "C" int main(int argc, char** argv)

with main linked to app_main. argc/argv are the invocation arguments the OS passes. The Arduino-style setup()/loop() runtime is layered on top of this entry by the SDK’s app-runtime shim, so apps that prefer that shape keep the same export.
Who owns the world

The app owns its code, its static data, and its calls into the host.
The host owns all hardware, all SDK singletons, the memory manager the app allocates from, and the thread that runs the app’s entry nightly.
Nothing is statically linked into the app (-nostdlib, undefined references resolved at load). Any symbol the app uses that is not defined inside it must be in the host export table, or load fails the pm check surface (see symbols).

Build-time version macros (PM_SDK_VERSION_*) are baked into the app; the host exports the matching pocketmage_sdk_version string/runtime parts it was built against. An app compares its own compile-time version against the host’s export to present a compatible pair.
APP_INIT
Apps receive one startup hook:
void APP_INIT();   // defined by the app, invoked by the entry shim

The OS/SDK host reaches APP_INIT() after peripheral and singleton bring-up (displays, FS, clock, i18n, …), so an app may read settings, open files, and prep its first screen there. The hook is also where boot-time apps decide whether to relaunch their UI at power-on.
Interactive lifetime
While running, the app owns the loop:

Poll input: pm_kb_read() for a keypress, pm_kb_state() for the current modifier state.
Draw: build the E-Ink buffer, refresh once, draw OLED text.
Sleep on idle: the host skips the idle timeout while an ELF app runs. Avoid poking the host idle timer and call pocketmage::deepSleep() explicitly when you want to enter deep sleep.

There is no cooperative yield handshake: the app either returns, sleeps, or keeps its own loop going. A CPU-heavy loop starves the WiFi and E-Ink tasks; prefer pocketmage::ScopedCpuBoost for short bursts and yield with delay() between frames.
Exiting
return 0;   // plain exit; control returns to the OS cleanly

Exiting is a return from main. There is no reboot handoff and no exit API. The loader tears down the app context, restores HOME, and repaints. A crashing app (fault, uncaught aborts) follows the same OS recovery path as the built-in apps (recoverFromCrash); the device boots back to HOME rather than leaving the app stuck.
Built-in vs third-party
The OS’s HOME, TXT, and friends are compiled-in apps that live entirely on the host side. Third-party apps are the ELF path described here. Both inhabit the same lib/PocketMage_SDK API, so the same app code

288.title: Publishing an app
288.text:
Publishing an app
The delivery unit is a plain .tar file placed in /apps/ on the device SD card and installed through APPLOADER on the device. Not gzipped, not a directory of loose files: one tar.
make pack (or pm pack) produces it. The tar’s top level must hold the members the installer keys off:



Member
Required
Meaning




<name>.app.elf
yes
the app binary (the *.app.elf suffix is detected)


<name>.elfo
yes
the overlay sidecar paged into exec RAM at load (see overlay.md)


<name>_ICON.bin
no
40x40 1-bit icon, 200 bytes


app.properties
no
name/version/author/scope manifest, copied to the slot (see app-abi.md)



<name> is the base of the ELF filename and becomes the app’s display name. Keep it short and unique; it is also the assets/ subdir name and the slot subdirectory.
Install behavior (APPLOADER)

Extract /apps/<name>.tar into /apps/temp, skipping macOS ._* junk.
Find the first *.app.elf, derive base by stripping .app.elf.
Find <base>_ICON.bin anywhere in the extracted tree (case-insensitive). A missing icon is non-fatal; the default is shown instead.
If an assets/ directory is present, copy it into /assets/<base> (flattened, best effort).
Install the ELF, its .elfo sidecar, the icon, and app.properties (when present) into the selected slot (/apps/slot<n>, 4 slots) and record metadata for the launcher and app switcher.

Slots are swapped wholesale: installing over a slot replaces its content and clears stale legacy metadata for that slot. After a successful install, delete the tar from /apps to free space on the card.
Icon
<name>_ICON.bin is 200 bytes: a 40x40, 1-bit-per-pixel bitmap, 5 bytes per row, 8 pixels per byte, MSB first. A set bit is black ink on the e-ink display. An absent icon shows the OS default; build with one so the launcher looks right.
Assets
An optional top-level assets/ directory in the tar is copied flat into /assets/<name> at install. Apps read their files from there at runtime. Nested directories and macOS metadata files inside assets/ are tolerated (metadata is skipped), but a flat layout is the reliable path.
Before you ship

Build from a clean checkout with the pinned toolchain: make --no-print-directory -C <app> clean all check pack, or pm build --clean --pack && pm check.
Inspect the artifact before shipping: tar -tvf build/<name>.tar and readelf -h on the ELF. The tar must list the ELF and the .elfo sidecar.
Don’t create the tar from your mac’s Finder copies: ._* files get skipped by the installer, but they bloat the package. make pack avoids it.
Don’t ship a .bin or the old OTA-style package. Production devices only install /apps/*.tar.

See also

App ABI - the manifest fields and the entry contract.
pm CLI - the commands that build and pack.

295.title: Rendering
295.text:
Rendering
PocketMage drives two panels from one shared app API. Getting pixel messages to the right panel and knowing when a refresh actually happens is the core of any screen.
Two targets, one FontEngine-dominated path

The OLED (256x32 SSD1326) is a fast status text panel. Apps reach it through pm_oled_send, pm_oled_sysmsg, and pm_oled_set_power_save.
The E-Ink (320x240 lambda) is the big document/list panel. Apps draw it with pm_eink_pixel, pm_eink_rect, and pm_eink_refresh, plus the frames engine and the ui helpers.

Every FontEngine call takes an explicit DisplayTarget, so the same measure/draw code works for both panels and the metrics are per-target. The OLED draw color and the E-Ink draw color are independent (font).
The E-Ink refresh model
The E-Ink driver is buffered: draw calls only write to the current buffer; nothing reaches the panel until a refresh() (or a full -ForceFull update). The canonical app rhythm is:
beginEinkScreen();                    // clear buffer, set full window
// ... FontEngine / EINK / ui draws ...
endEinkScreen("Status text");         // draw status band + refresh

beginEinkScreen(preserveBg) optionally keeps the previous buffer background (for scrolling windows) instead of clearing. endEinkScreen adds the status bar for you. If you manage the window yourself, call pm_eink_refresh() directly; PM_REFRESH_FORCE_FULL exists for content that must not ghost.
Status band ownership: the bottom kEinkStatusH (26) pixels belong to drawStatusBar. Content frames should stay within kEinkContentH (214) (layout).
Text metrics and layout

y in draw calls is the baseline, not the top.
Fit text before drawing: pm_text_width + sliceThatFits, or truncateWithEllipsis for a single line; wordWrap for paragraphs (layout).
Row pitch is einkRowPitch(style) = font height + line spacing; Normal-vs-ForceFull refresh choice rides on pm_eink_get_line_spacing().
Named constants (kFrameTextPadX, kOledWordBaseline, kOledInfoBaseline, kGridLabelMaxW, …) are in layout; use them instead of literals.

The scroll loop
These three views share one gesture-sensing core (touch):

Fixed window with offset: pm_touch_update_scroll_from_touch(), then read pm_touch_get_dynamic_scroll() and draw the sliding window. Used by TXT.
Step scroll: pm_touch_update_scroll(maxScroll, lineScroll, step), redraw only when it returns true. Used by lists.
Gesture vector: pm_touch_get_scroll_vector() for preview-band feedback (t >= 1 scrolls by a page).

OLED overlay patterns
For transient feedback use pm_oled_sysmsg(text, ms); it draws a framed dialog over whatever the E-Ink is showing and dismisses itself. Long text that the OLED cannot hold goes wider than the widget: pass longer strings only when they fit the panel, or refresh a region for a running thumbnail of the E-Ink window.
Full examples
pm new myapp gives the text-only skeleton. For draw-heavy apps, start from the same template and call the E-Ink and OLED functions directly; see app-abi.md for what the app process owns.

303.title: Internationalization (i18n)
303.text:
Internationalization (i18n)
The SDK carries the translation engine, the generator tooling, and the base catalog of SDK-owned strings. An app brings its own catalog. At build time the catalogs merge into a single enum and one set of string tables per firmware image.
Layout
PocketMage_SDK/
  pocketmage_i18n/
    pocketmage_i18n.h / .cpp          # runtime engine (I18n class)
    languages/                        # base catalog (SDK-owned strings)
      en/pocketmage_i18n.po
      fr/pocketmage_i18n.po
      fr/pocketmage_i18n.aliases
      es/...  de/...
    tools/
      gen_i18n.py                     # merger, generator, and build hook
    tests/
      test_gen_i18n.py

An app adds one catalog directory of its own:
<app>/src/i18n/
  en/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.aliases
  ...

A catalog directory has one subdirectory per language, named by the language code. en is required and defines that catalog’s string order.
Catalog format
Standard gettext .po. msgctxt is the StringID enum name; msgid is the English text; msgstr is the translation. The en file carries a # Languages: directive in its leading comment block:
# PocketMage OS English Translations
# Languages: en fr es de

msgctxt "STR_SYS_HELLO"
msgid "Hello"
msgstr "Hello"

That directive, in the base catalog, is where the language list and order come from. Each catalog’s en file defines the order of the strings that catalog contributes; the catalog’s other languages must list the same msgctxts, with the same msgids, in the same order.
A language missing from a catalog falls back to that catalog’s English text, so an English-only app catalog is valid without translating anything.
Aliases
pocketmage_i18n.aliases maps folded, lowercase user input to a StringID. Optional, only defined for non-English languages:
annuler -> STR_KB_APP_CANCEL

Folding strips diacritics (Paramètres -> parametres). Aliases from all catalogs concatenate per language; a key that folds to the same value twice is a build error.
Ownership



Owner
Namespaces




SDK base catalog
STR_KB_* (incl. STR_KB_APP_*, STR_KB_USB_*, STR_KB_INIT_*), STR_GRID_*, STR_SD_*, STR_WIFI_*, STR_SYS_*, STR_TOUCHPAD_*, STR_OLED_*, STR_FRAME(S)_*, STR_INFO/GOOD/SAVED_*, STR_DAY_*, STR_MONTH_*


App catalog
STR_TERM_*, STR_ONBOARD_*, STR_SSH_*, STR_SETTINGS_*, STR_CAL_*, STR_UTILS_*, STR_LOCK_*, STR_HOME_*, STR_TASKS_*, STR_FILEWIZ_*, STR_APPLOADER_*, STR_COMM_*, STR_USB_*, STR_LEX_*, STR_JOURNAL_*, STR_TXT_*, STR_GOTO_*, STR_SAVE_*



msgctxt names are globally unique across the merged catalogs; reusing one the SDK already defines is a build error. SDK code only references SDK namespaces, so merging an app catalog never changes how SDK code behaves.
Ownership follows the consumer: base if SDK code references the string, app otherwise. That keeps a bare SDK checkout building standalone (its base catalog contains every string its own modules use), and the merge appends the app catalog after the base, so app strings never move base enum values. The indexed helper ranges all sit in the base; their relative order is fixed and never perturbed by an app catalog.
Generator
tools/gen_i18n.py merges the catalogs in command-line order and writes pocketmage_i18n_gen.h and pocketmage_i18n_gen.cpp:
python3 pocketmage_i18n/tools/gen_i18n.py \
    --catalog pocketmage_i18n/languages \
    --catalog ../app/src/i18n \
    --out-dir <build-dir>

--catalog is repeatable; the first catalog is the base. With no arguments, the tool generates the SDK’s own base catalog into pocketmage_i18n/, so a bare SDK checkout builds standalone.
The merge keeps base strings first and appends each later catalog in turn. Every enum value equals its index in the merged order, so the layout is stable: adding an app catalog never changes SDK string values.
Validation
The generator exits non-zero and aborts the build on any of:

a missing # Languages: directive in the base en file, or en not first;
a msgctxt that is not [A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*;
a duplicate msgctxt within a catalog or across catalogs;
a non-en file whose msgctxt set, order, or msgids differ from that catalog’s en;
a duplicated folded alias;
the indexed helper ranges missing, inverted, overlapping, or out of order.

Indexed helper ranges
Four ranges are indexed by the runtime helpers (appName(), dayName(), monthName(), kbAppName()). They must stay contiguous blocks, in this order:



Range
Members




STR_KB_APP_CANCEL … STR_KB_APP_LOADER
app list in the keyboard app switcher


STR_GRID_TXT … STR_GRID_LOADER
app list in the launcher grid


STR_DAY_SUNDAY … STR_DAY_SATURDAY
weekdays


STR_MONTH_JAN … STR_MONTH_ERR
months (ERR is the last member)



Their heads are emitted with explicit = N enum values as documentation of intent; the values always equal the index in the merged order.
Build integration
The generator doubles as the build hook. Point extra_scripts at it in the app’s platformio.ini; it reads its set

325.title: Migrating an existing app
325.text:
Migrating an existing app
Production devices no longer run apps built the old way. An app is now a runtime-loaded ELF shipped as /apps/*.tar; there is no firmware-flashing app flow and no OTA-style app package on production.
The short version: if you shipped an app pre-ELF, that package will not launch on production firmware. Rebuild it against the ELF contract and re-package.
What changed



Aspect
Old flow
New flow




Binary
monolithic app inside the firmware image
standalone ET_DYN ELF


Delivery
firmware .bin / OTA-style app package
/apps/<name>.tar on the SD card, installed via APPLOADER


Instantiation
compiled in, launched by the OS
loaded in-process when launched, torn down on return


Dependencies
linked into the firmware build
resolved from the host at load time (-nostdlib)


Toolchain
PlatformIO (big-endian)
espressif xtensa-esp-elf


Layout/naming
app id / metadata
derived from the tar base name



The OS keeps app code out of PSRAM by design; code runs from IRAM. That is the loader’s job, not yours.
Migration steps

Get the toolchain. Install the espressif xtensa-esp-elf toolchain into ~/.espressif/... as shown in build.md. Do not rely on the PlatformIO toolchain; it emits big-endian ELFs the loader cannot read.
Scaffold. Run pm new myapp. Its Makefile (include tools/app.mk) is the whole build system.
Port the entry. Wrap your start logic in extern "C" int main(int, char**). The build renames it to app_main. Fit the previous app’s lifetime to the return-from-main model (app-abi.md).
Replace dependencies. Every call must resolve at load time. Host exports are the curated surface in symbols.md plus the host’s newlib/IDF/Arduino globals. That covers display, keyboard, buzzer, clock, IO, and the standard library. If you depended on app-side firmware globals that are not exported, move that dependency to API calls.
Move assets. Files the app used at compile time become a top-level assets/ directory in the tar, read at runtime from /assets/<name> (publishing).
Localize. If the app contained strings, move them into an app catalog (src/i18n/, merged per i18n.md) instead of hardcoding.
Verify. make clean all check must succeed, list a sane set of undefined symbols, and the endianness check must pass. Then make pack and tar -tvf build/<name>.tar.
Ship. Copy the tar to /apps/ on the device, install with APPLOADER into a slot, launch. The launcher shows the name and icon drawn from the package.

Gotchas

Big-endian artifacts. The classic failure. The loader does no byte swapping, so a PlatformIO-built app faults at load with a section or instruction fault. readelf -h shows big endian before you ship.
Statically linked runtime. Symbols collide or bloat; keep -nostdlib.
Relying on slot directories. After install the ELF lives in the slot dir, but the app should treat /assets/<name> (copied at install) as its data home and never assume the slot path.
Long-lived loops. The app shares the device. Cooperative lifetimes (render, yield via the SDK API, return) beat spin loops on the 16 KB run stack.

Announcement
If you maintained published apps pre-ELF, publish a migration notice: existing packages targeting production will not launch on the new firmware, and step 8 above is the path forward.

331.title: Overlay format (.elfo)
331.text:
Overlay format (.elfo)
Every packed app carries two artifacts: the relocatable <name>.app.elf and a sidecar <name>.elfo. The ELF is the program; the ELFO blob is the overlay image the host pages into executable RAM at load time. The build produces the .elfo automatically (see build.md); this page documents what it contains and how the loader consumes it, so the format is pinned contract rather than an implementation detail.
The overlay runtime lives in the elf_overlay component, an ISA-abstracted overlay loader that sits next to the ELF loader (esp_elf) and handles the parts of loading that a plain relocating loader cannot: paging .text bodies into a fixed pool of executable frames and patching ISA-specific PC-relative literal loads once the resident addresses are known.
Why it exists
An ELF app links -nostdlib -shared and resolves every symbol from the host at load time (see app-abi.md and symbols.md). On the ESP32-S3 the loader must place executable code in memory that the instruction bus can fetch (MALLOC_CAP_EXEC), which is scarce. Mapping an entire app image into exec RAM wastes that budget on code paths that may never run.
The overlay model solves this. Instead of loading all .text up front, the host relocates the base image with esp_elf, then pages individual overlay bodies into a small pool of exec-RAM frames on demand. A function that is never called is never paged in. The .elfo blob is the pre-chewed form the device needs for that: the overlay bodies, the stub block that enters and leaves them, and the relocation patch tables the host applies once it knows where each frame landed.
PC-relative literal loads (l32r on Xtensa, auipc on RISC-V) cannot be left to the base relocator, because the literal’s absolute address is not known until the overlay body is resident. elf_overlay patches those in place at page-in. The base relocator never touches them.
On-disk layout
The blob begins with the four-byte magic ELFO, format version 1, and an ISA tag. All multi-byte fields are little-endian, matching the app ELF. The header is followed by fixed-shape tables and two data regions:
flowchart TB
    H["elf_overlay_header_t<br>magic ELFO, version, ISA tag, table counts"]
    O["overlay entries<br>id, offset, length (one per overlay body)"]
    S["stub entries<br>canonical vaddr, overlay_id, body_offset, stub_off"]
    R["redirect entries<br>call site, stub_off"]
    P["patch entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset"]
    SP["stub_patch entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset"]
    HR["host_ref entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset, name_off"]
    ST["string table<br>null-terminated host symbol names"]
    SB["stub block<br>enter/leave slots plus stub code"]
    B["overlay bodies<br>verbatim .text images"]
    H --> O --> S --> R --> P --> SP --> HR --> ST --> SB --> B




Table
What it records




overlay
Each overlay body’s id, its offset into the bodies region, and length.


stub
Maps a canonical .text virtual address to the stub that enters it.


redirect
Resident call sites that must be patched to jump through a stub.


patch
ISA literal-load sites inside overlay bodies, patched at page-in.


stub_patch
ISA literal-load sites inside the stub block.


host_ref
Overlay references to host symbols, resolved by name via the resolver.


string table
The host symbol names the host_ref entries point into.



All tables are fixed-size records, so parsing and page-in do no heap allocation beyond the frame pool itself.
ISA abstraction
ISA-specific patching lives behind elf_overlay_isa_ops_t. Two backends are registered:

xtensa - l32r PC-relative literal patching, validated against the Xtensa ISA reference. This is the backend PocketMage uses on the S3.
riscv - auipc PC-relative literal patching.

The ISA tag in the header selects the backend at load time. A blob built for one ISA will not load on another.
How the host consumes it
The in-process runner (src/elf_runner.cpp) loads an app in two stages: the base relocation with esp_elf, then the overlay with elf_overlay. The exact sequence, matching the code:

Install the scoped symbol resolver (see symbols.md), then esp_elf_init and esp_elf_relocate_source relocate the base image. The image is streamed by offset from the SD file rather than held whole in RAM.
Locate the .elfo sidecar next to the ELF and elf_overlay_load it.
elf_overlay_set_active makes it the active overlay for the run.
elf_overlay_esp_elf_set_section_map copies the relocated section table (canonical virtual address to resident address) from the esp_elf_t into the overlay’s section map.
elf_overlay_apply_redirects patches the resident call sites so calls into paged functions go through their stubs.
elf_overlay_set_symbol_resolver wires host-reference resolution back through the scoped

342.title: Symbols and the dependency contract
342.text:
Symbols and the dependency contract
Apps link -nostdlib. Nothing ships with the binary that satisfies a reference; at load time the host resolves every undefined symbol from its own live memory. The app’s undefined-symbol list is therefore its real dependency contract. make check prints it; pm check interprets it against the host surface.
The surface
An app can call anything the host exports as a global symbol. The export surface has two curated parts, backed by two committed lists at the SDK root:

symbols.list - the PocketMage pm_* ABI plus a handful of host primitives. Its pm_* block is generated; do not hand edit it (see below).
host_baseline.list - the C/C++ runtime, newlib, and POSIX symbols the firmware exports unconditionally. Apps may rely on these without listing them. Generated from the firmware’s export table; do not hand edit it.

The pm gate reads both lists and takes their union as the curated surface (tools/pm/gate.py:read_curated). An undefined symbol in an app must appear in that union, or be confirmed present in a supplied host ELF, for the app to pass.
The C and C++ runtime. libc, libm, libgcc, libstdc++ and libsupc++ symbols the firmware already links are exported so apps can use third-party libraries, and host_baseline.list records them. tools/symbols.py derives this set by reading the toolchain archives with nm and keeping the symbols that are present in the firmware image:
python3 tools/symbols.py --list symbols.list --host-elf <firmware.elf> \
  --print-cost

libc        250 symbols   4,467 bytes
libm         15 symbols     262 bytes
libstdc++    87 symbols   3,403 bytes
libsupc++    58 symbols   2,362 bytes
libgcc       65 symbols   1,552 bytes
libnewlib    94 symbols   2,478 bytes
total       602 symbols  15,009 bytes (14.7 KB)

That total includes the curated pm_* entries. The runtime adds about 11.2 KB of flash in the firmware image, once. It is not a per-app cost. Apps stay small: a hello world is 1.3 KB, an app using std::vector and std::string is 2.3 KB, an app with cJSON linked in is 5.2 KB. --gc-sections and --strip-all in tools/app.mk do that work.
A symbol in symbols.list that the firmware does not define is reported as a warning but still emitted into the table. A newly added wrapper cannot appear in --host-elf until the host is rebuilt, so dropping it would omit it on the one run that adds it. Regenerate once more after building and the warning should be gone.
Runtime export is on by default. Pass --no-runtime to export only the curated SDK list, which restricts apps to the SDK surface and no libraries.
Membership is decided by which archive a symbol comes from, not by its name. A _ZN... prefix also matches the SDK’s own C++ classes, so matching on prefix shape would export firmware internals by accident.
GCC reserves __atomic_*, __sync_* and __builtin_* names as builtins and rejects taking their address. Those exports are declared under a private pm_elfsym_ identifier with an asm label, then listed by their literal name in the table.
The curated SDK table. symbols.list is PocketMage’s own export promise. Its pm_* block is generated by tools/gen_app_api.py, which walks the SDK headers, projects each C++ method to a C wrapper, and writes the wrapper names into both symbols.list (SDK side) and src/ELF_SYMS/host_exports.list (OS side) so the two can never drift. tools/symbols.py is a different tool: it derives the runtime baseline above from the toolchain archives. Host-side, host_exports.list tracks a superset of symbols.list, validated against the firmware image. Both lists feed the same generated g_customer_elfsyms table.
Do not hand edit the pm_* block of symbols.list. To change the app-facing surface, change the SDK header and regenerate with gen_app_api.py; it rewrites the generated files together.
Linking a third-party library
A vendored library’s source is compiled into the app by overriding APP_SRCS. Anything the library references that is not in the app is resolved by the host at load time. Two consequences are worth knowing.
Libraries compiled at -Os need fewer symbols than the same source at -O0. A std::vector<std::string> app at -O0 wants 13 symbols including std::allocator<char> constructors; at -Os it wants 7, and all 7 resolve.
sscanf is not exported by default. It exists in newlib, but nothing in the firmware references it, so it was dropped by --gc-sections, and referencing it pulls in about 190 KB of stdio reentrancy. A library that needs it must either avoid it or the host must export it deliberately.
Reading an app’s contract
make check   # prints entry + every undefined symbol
pm check     # classifies each symbol and exits non-zero on a broken contract

Everything in that list must exist in the host’s global view when the app loads, or the load fails. pm check with --host-elf is the exact gate: every undefined symbol must resolve to a host global.
Without a host ELF, pm check reads the generated export table that the firmware links,

350.title: Troubleshooting
350.text:
Troubleshooting
The failure modes below are the ones an app build or load actually hits. Each entry names the symptom, the cause, and the fix. The deeper references are linked from each.
Build and toolchain
XTENSA_CXX not found, or the wrong compiler is used
The build probes for the espressif xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++ and falls back to the PlatformIO package and PATH. If it picks the PlatformIO package, the link output has the wrong byte order and the endianness guard deletes it (see below). Pin the compiler explicitly:
make XTENSA_CXX=~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-15.2.0_20251204/xtensa-esp-elf/bin/xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++

Confirm what the build resolved with make pm-info. The install steps are in toolchain.md.
The build fails with an endianness assertion and deletes the artifact
app.mk asserts little-endian output after every link and removes a big-endian artifact so a bad file never ships. This almost always means the wrong toolchain compiled the app. Only the espressif xtensa-esp-elf toolchain emits readable output; the PlatformIO Xtensa package does not. Fix the toolchain, not the guard.
elf_overlay_relink or elf_overlay_emit not found
The .elfo overlay sidecar is built by two host tools that must be on PATH. Build them from an elf_overlay checkout and add the build directory to PATH, or point ELF_OVERLAY_RELINK and ELF_OVERLAY_EMIT at the binaries. See toolchain.md.
A single function will not fit in an overlay frame
An overlay body must fit in one frame of the executable-RAM pool (ELF_OVERLAY_DEFAULT_FRAME_SIZE, default 16 KB). A single function larger than a frame cannot be paged in. Split the function. See overlay.md.
Gating (pm check)
Symbols reported as “broken” / “not resolvable by the host”
The app references a symbol the host does not export. The load would fail. The symbol must be added to the SDK’s curated surface before an app can use it, or the app must stop referencing it. The symbol model is in symbols.md.
Symbols reported as “unconfirmed”
The symbol sits outside the curated surface (symbols.list plus host_baseline.list), so pm check cannot confirm it without the actual host export table. Re-run with --host-elf <firmware.elf> for an exact result.
Warning: app_main is not in the ELF’s symbol table
Not a failure. The post-link strip removed the app_main name, but the entry is linker-pinned with -e app_main, so the loader still finds it. Ignore it.
Warning: the app has a non-empty .init_array
The app links static constructors. The host’s esp_elf loader does not run relocation-time constructors, so they never execute. Remove the static construction, or move the initialization into app_main. The compile flags -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics are on by default to keep this from happening; a remaining .init_array usually comes from a global with a non-trivial constructor. See app-abi.md.
pm tooling
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tools' when running pm
The pm command was installed editable (pip install -e) against a checkout that has since moved or been deleted, so its link to the tools package is dead. A common trigger is installing from a temporary scaffold directory that the OS later cleaned up. Current pm builds detect this and offer to reinstall; if you see the raw error, the installed CLI predates the resilient launcher. Reinstall against a live checkout:
pm update-sdk --sdk /path/to/PocketMage_SDK

If pm itself will not start, run the equivalent reinstall directly with the interpreter that owns the pm script:
/path/to/that/python -m pip install -e /path/to/PocketMage_SDK

Run pm doctor afterward to confirm the install is healthy.
pm behaves differently from the SDK checkout you are editing
The installed CLI is a different version from the checkout. pm doctor reports the version skew. Reinstall to re-sync:
pm update-sdk

An editable install avoids this in the first place, because the CLI tracks the checkout it was linked to. See the install notes.
Load-time (on device)
ELF needs symbols outside its scope
The app’s app.properties manifest declares a scope that does not include a pm_* symbol the app actually calls, so the scoped resolver refuses to resolve it and the load fails fast. Widen the scope (default all) to cover the API the app uses, or stop calling the out-of-scope API. Only pm_* symbols are gated by scope; the runtime baseline is always reachable. See symbols.md.
The app loads but runs unredirected / behaves oddly on large code paths
The .elfo sidecar was not found next to the ELF, so the app ran from the base relocation alone without the overlay. Confirm the tar shipped the .elfo member (tar -tf build/<name>.tar) and that the installer placed it in the slot. See overlay.md.
The app never returns control
Returning from app_main is how an app exits: the overlay is unloaded, the base image deinitialized, and HOME reopens. An app that never returns leaks the run task. A UI app must hand control back cooperatively and then return. See app-abi.md
